newsitem.title: USA: Agents sift dirt for Atlanta bomb clues.
newsitem.headline: Agents sift dirt for Atlanta bomb clues.

text.p: Investigators on Saturday sifted dirt from the site of two powerful bomb blasts as workers retrieved belongings from the badly damaged building housing an abortion clinic that was possibly the bombers' target.
Federal agents used large screens to search through shovelfuls of dirt in a hunt for clues and minute fragments of the bombs that exploded on Thursday at a suburban Atlanta office building.

People who worked there carted bags full of files, computer equipment and ledgers from the three-story Sandy Springs Professional Building, where the bombs blasted out windows and walls and brought down sections of ceiling.
"There are no windows. There are obviously walls down," said Mili Boreham, a personnel consultant, as she emerged from the complex with bags of belongings. "A lot of glass needs to be cleaned up."
The bombings rocked the Atlanta Northside Family Planning Services centre, the same clinic that was the target of Atlanta's last abortion clinic bombing 13 years ago.
The manner in which the bombs exploded, about an hour apart, led to speculation that the bomber intended to lure police, firefighters and investigators to the scene in order to harm or kill them.
A group of local fire chiefs offered a $15,000 reward for information leading to arrests. No suspect has been arrested.
"We feel the secondary device detonated was deliberately intended to injure or kill firefighters and public safety officers," Clayton County Fire Chief Glenn Johnson said.

Authorities, concerned about the integrity of the investigation, have said little about the nature of the two bombs, describing them only as "very powerful" and saying that it was fortunate no one was killed.
But in three days since the bombing, a clearer picture has emerged.
Television video taken from above the site of the second bomb, on the edge of a parking lot next to a garbage container, shows a large crater and two cars that were virtually demolished by the blast.
U.S. Attorney Kent Alexander said the cars had probably prevented deaths by absorbing much of the power of the bomb.

John Morton, a retired Army munitions expert who was near the building when the first bomb went off, said he estimated it was a 30- to 40-pound (13-18 kilogram) charge, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported on Saturday.

The two bombs, besides causing extensive damage to the building and destroying the cars, blew out plate glass windows in an adjacent office building and cracked windows in businesses several hundred yards (metres) away. Shrapnel was found on the roof of the adjacent building.

A state investigator reported finding nails in the building. Fox television affiliate WAGA, citing unnamed sources, reported the second bomb was "packed with nails" intended to become "deadly projectiles" when the device went off.
Other local media reported the bombs may have been constructed of dynamite and blasting caps.

Though authorities would only say the clinic was a "possible" target, business owners and workers at the Sandy Springs complex say the bombings had given them second thoughts about sharing a building with an abortion clinic and some indicated they may move if the clinic reopens.
"It will depend on what the investigation determines," Boreham said. "I want to be able to come and go and not worry about whether I'm going to die."
A number of Atlanta abortion clinics had hired private security guards and local law enforcement remained on heightened alert, conducting sweeps of clinics to deter copycats and ensure worker safety.
None of the six people taken to hospitals in the wake of the bombing was seriously hurt. The FBI agent who had remained in a local hospital for testing was released late on Friday.
